reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its primary purpose is teaching GTA Online players how to acquire properties and complete missions or heists for in-game payouts. The visuals show an in-game property browser and payout screens for named GTA heists. Although it uses rapid-wealth language and mentions cheap Shark Cards, the described material does not show a request for money, credentials, or participation in a deceptive external offer.

citations.quote: ZERO to MILLIONS | The Ultimate Guide for NEW and BROKE Players of GTA Online | Get RICH Fast
This video will teach how to go from absolutely broke to making millions in just five easy stages.
Each stage will be dedicated to obtaining the funds for the different property purchases that will unlock various content to be used in the next stage.
contact missions can be done solo which is great, but you'll get a higher payout always if you do them with friends

opening.argument: Judge, the promised outcome is explicit: going from broke to millions in five easy stages. [DESCRIPTION_0001] The path is tied to purchases: the speaker says each stage obtains funds for properties that unlock the next stage's content. [ASR_0002] Alongside that path, the description offers a link labeled “Cheap Shark Cards.” [DESCRIPTION_0001] The issue is not whether missions can pay in-game money; it is whether a beginner-facing promise of rapid asset acquisition, paired with a purchase pathway, should be treated as mere instruction. The material does not establish what happens after a viewer follows that external link.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's mission examples explain one route to in-game payouts, but they do not account for the separate “Cheap Shark Cards” link. [DESCRIPTION_0001] Nor does the absence of a spoken request to pay establish what the linked offer asks viewers to do. The concern is the pairing of a beginner-focused wealth promise with an external purchase link, not a claim that the gameplay itself is fabricated.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: That pairing does not establish a scam solicitation. The speaker gives a concrete in-game route: contact missions have stated payouts, and VIP missions have stated payouts even when played solo. [ASR_0003] The description lists a Shark Cards link, but supplies no claim that using it is required to earn the promised in-game money, or evidence about the linked offer's terms. [DESCRIPTION_0001]

opening.argument: The warning signs deserve consideration together. The title advertises “ZERO to MILLIONS” and “Get RICH Fast” to new and broke players. [TITLE_0001] The description compresses that outcome into “five easy stages” and includes a shortened link for “Cheap Shark Cards.” [DESCRIPTION_0001] The video also displays large base-payout figures. [F0053] Each element can have an innocent gaming explanation. Together, however, they make rapid acquisition feel accessible while placing an external purchasing option near the promise. A judge should not dismiss the solicitation risk solely because the amounts are denominated in the game's currency.

opening.argument: The instructional format also steers viewers toward acquiring assets. The speaker calls a $1.75 million Buzzard “worth every penny” because it helps with VIP missions, then recommends saving for a Doomsday facility. [ASR_0011] The description supplies a “Cheap Shark Cards” link. [DESCRIPTION_0001] Those details matter together: the lesson repeatedly establishes desirable, costly in-game purchases while an external purchasing route sits beside it. The gameplay explanation may be genuine, but genuine instruction can still promote a questionable acquisition path. The supplied material does not show the terms of that linked path, so the defense cannot verify it from the tutorial alone.
